fixes.title: Read each answer in context
fixes.root_cause: The AI read each answer in isolation. When an expert said “we”, “their” or “the board”, it didn't know which company they meant, so it couldn't tell that the expert was talking about their own employer, a client or a former employer.

examples.name: Priya Natarajan
examples.quote: For us specifically, we're moving list price up 12% on the mid-market tier from January. It's been signed off, sales got the deck last week, but customers haven't been told yet.

examples.name: Henrik Lindqvist
examples.quote: The board approved the sale of the European tyre business on Tuesday. The announcement is planned for after the half-year results.

examples.name: Olivia Grant
examples.highlight: the regulator's decision on their diabetes drug
examples.quote: Between us, the regulator's decision on their diabetes drug came back last week, and it's a rejection. They haven't announced it yet.

how: Give the AI the expert's declaration and the question asked alongside every answer.
Work out which company “we”, “our” or “their” refers to before judging the answer.
Check what was said against the expert's restrictions and the date they left each company.

fixes.title: Check for people and sources, not just companies
fixes.root_cause: The AI only looked for information about companies. It didn't catch private individuals being named, or experts naming insiders as their source.

examples.name: Elena Vasquez
examples.highlight: My contact Jamie Holt, who runs procurement there now, told me
examples.quote: My contact Jamie Holt, who runs procurement there now, told me last week they're giving notice to two of them in Q1.

examples.name: Hannah Booth
examples.quote: I remember Mark Ellison, who led their financial crime team at the time, was signed off for months with a breakdown afterwards.

how: Flag any named private individual mentioned alongside health, family or legal details.
Flag phrases that point to an inside source, such as “my contact”, “told me” and “I still speak to”.
Send both to a reviewer, with the name highlighted.

fixes.title: Check the expert's cited source before flagging
fixes.cause_label: Why the AI raised a false alarm
fixes.root_cause: Most false alarms were statements the expert attributed to a public source, such as an earnings call, a press release or an annual report. The AI flagged them without checking whether the information really was public.

Check that source: filings, press releases or the company's website.
Clear the statement if the information is there. Keep it flagged if it isn't.

missed-sanjay-mehta.profile: Sanjay Mehta. Finance Director, Northwind Biomedical (2018 to March 2026). Independent consultant (March 2026 to present). Industry: medical devices.
missed-sanjay-mehta.declaration: Left Northwind Biomedical (listed company) in March 2026. No current employer in medical devices. Standard confidentiality obligations to Northwind. No conflicts declared.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Sanjay, thanks for your time. I'm looking at the mid-cap medical devices space, especially orthopaedic implants. How is demand?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Strong. Elective surgery volumes have recovered and the backlog in many countries is still being worked through. Ageing populations make the long-term demand very predictable.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: How about pricing?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Under pressure from hospital procurement, especially in Europe where tenders are aggressive. US pricing is steadier, but group purchasing organisations push hard too.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: What about Northwind specifically?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: I'll stay careful there since I only left in March. Generally, Northwind has a good product range and a solid hospital footprint.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Anything investors should be aware of?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Look, I'm not saying anything specific, but if I were you I'd watch their Q3 numbers closely. Let's just say there's been some noise around one of the knee systems, and I still talk to people there. Quality issues take a while to show up in the numbers.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Okay. Going back to the market, how important is regulation?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Very. The EU medical device regulation raised the bar for clinical evidence. Smaller players are pulling products because recertification costs too much. That's good for the bigger, well-capitalised companies.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: And robotics in orthopaedics?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: It's the main arms race. Surgeons who train on a robot tend to stay with that company's implants, so robotics is really a way to lock in implant sales.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Thank you, Sanjay.

missed-sanjay-mehta.reviewer_comment: Hedged, but points to a possible undisclosed product quality issue at a listed former employer, sourced from current contacts there. Too uncertain for AI to clear or reject; needs a compliance reviewer.
missed-sanjay-mehta.root_cause: The AI looks for named companies, and none is named: the expert says “their”. Linking it to Northwind, a listed company he left in March 2026, needs the question before it and his declaration.
missed-sanjay-mehta.name: Sanjay Mehta
missed-sanjay-mehta.role: Finance Director, Northwind Biomedical (2018 to March 2026). Independent consultant (March 2026 to present).

missed-olivia-grant.profile: Olivia Grant. Regulatory Affairs Manager, Pellham Biosciences (2016 to 2022). Principal Consultant, Ashgrove Regulatory Partners (2022 to present). Industry: pharmaceuticals, regulatory affairs.
missed-olivia-grant.declaration: Currently a consultant at Ashgrove Regulatory Partners, which advises listed drug developers on regulatory submissions; Torvane Pharma (listed company) is a current client. Must not discuss any client's non-public regulatory, clinical or commercial information.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Thanks for joining, Olivia. I'm looking at diabetes and weight-loss drugs, and how regulators are treating the newer once-weekly treatments. Where are we in the cycle?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: We're in a busy phase. After the first wave of once-weekly injectables, regulators have a clearer template for what they want to see, so submissions are better prepared. The questions have moved on from whether these drugs work to long-term safety, especially heart outcomes and muscle loss.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: How long are reviews taking at the moment?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Standard reviews are running close to the published timelines, roughly a year. Where it slips is when the regulator asks for more data mid-review. That can add six months, and smaller companies often haven't budgeted for it.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: What tends to trigger those requests?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Usually the safety database is too small, or the trial population doesn't match the patients who'll actually get the drug. Manufacturing is the other one. Inspectors find problems at a contract manufacturer and the whole file stalls.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Torvane has its once-weekly diabetes drug under review. How do you rate their chances?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Between us, the regulator's decision on their diabetes drug came back last week, and it's a rejection. They haven't announced it yet.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Let's go back to the wider market. How are health systems responding to the price of these drugs?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Cautiously, in most of Europe. Health systems are limiting access to patients with the highest body mass index or existing heart disease, and pushing for deals linked to outcomes. Volumes will grow, but the price per patient will keep falling.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Thanks, Olivia.

missed-olivia-grant.reviewer_comment: The expert advises Torvane on its submissions and disclosed an unannounced regulatory rejection, which is plainly material and non-public. We redacted the passage, held the transcript back from the client and referred the expert to the vetting team.
missed-olivia-grant.root_cause: The AI assessed each expert turn on its own, and this turn names no company: 'their' points back to Torvane in the interviewer's question. Without that link it never matched the passage to the client listed in the declaration, and read 'the regulator's decision' as general regulatory commentary.
missed-olivia-grant.name: Olivia Grant
missed-olivia-grant.role: Regulatory Affairs Manager, Pellham Biosciences (2016 to 2022). Principal Consultant, Ashgrove Regulatory Partners (2022 to present).

missed-henrik-lindqvist.profile: Henrik Lindqvist. Plant Manager, Nordvik Rubber (2012 to 2019). Head of Corporate Strategy, Brannholt Automotive (2019 to present). Industry: automotive components and tyres.
missed-henrik-lindqvist.declaration: Currently employed by Brannholt Automotive (listed company), which owns a European tyre business. May discuss the tyre and components market in general. Must not discuss Brannholt's non-public information, financials, strategy or corporate activity.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Henrik, thanks for your time. I'm researching the European tyre market. How healthy is it right now?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Mixed. Replacement tyres are steady, because people keep driving older cars for longer. Volumes for new cars follow vehicle production, which is still below where it was before the pandemic. And Asian imports have taken a big share of the budget end.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: How are European producers responding to the imports?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: By moving up the range. Premium and large-rim tyres, winter and all-season, and tyres designed for electric vehicles, which carry more weight and need to run quietly. The budget segment is very hard to defend with European energy and labour costs.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Is there pressure to consolidate?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Yes. A lot of diversified component groups are asking whether they should own tyre plants at all. Tyres are capital heavy, and the margins are thinner than in electronics or software-rich parts.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Are any of the groups actually acting on that?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: The board approved the sale of the European tyre business on Tuesday. The announcement is planned for after the half-year results.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Moving on, how much are electric vehicles changing the replacement cycle?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Quite a lot. Electric cars are heavier and deliver torque instantly, so tyres wear faster, often 20 to 30% sooner. That's good for replacement volumes, and drivers seem willing to pay more for tyres approved for their car.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: And raw materials?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Natural rubber prices have been volatile, and the new European deforestation rules mean producers must trace rubber back to the plantation. That adds cost and favours the bigger groups that already have traceability systems.

missed-henrik-lindqvist.reviewer_comment: Henrik heads strategy at Brannholt, a listed company, and disclosed a board-approved sale of its European tyre business ahead of the announcement. We rejected the transcript and escalated the expert for breaching his declaration.
missed-henrik-lindqvist.root_cause: The expert said 'the board' rather than 'our board' and never named Brannholt, so the AI read the answer as commentary on consolidation among peers. The issue only shows against the declaration, which says he works in strategy at a listed group that owns a European tyre business, and the AI did not make that comparison.
missed-henrik-lindqvist.name: Henrik Lindqvist
missed-henrik-lindqvist.role: Plant Manager, Nordvik Rubber (2012 to 2019). Head of Corporate Strategy, Brannholt Automotive (2019 to present).

missed-nadia-rahimi.profile: Nadia Rahimi. Account Manager, Fenwick Cartons (2014 to 2018). Key Account Director, Stellan Packaging (2018 to August 2026). Independent packaging consultant (August 2026 to present). Industry: food and drink packaging.
missed-nadia-rahimi.declaration: Left Stellan Packaging (listed company) in August 2026. No current employer. Standard confidentiality obligations to Stellan, including its customer contracts. No conflicts declared.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Nadia, thanks for joining. I'm looking at packaging suppliers to the big food manufacturers. How do those contracts usually work?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Most large food companies run tenders every three to five years for their main packaging categories: cartons, films, trays. The contracts set volumes and a price formula, with pass-through clauses for board, resin and energy costs.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: How sticky are the customers?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Stickier than people think. Switching means new tooling, line trials and food safety sign-off, which can take most of a year. So incumbents usually keep the business unless service or quality has gone badly wrong.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: And how concentrated are the suppliers' customer books?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Very, for the mid-sized listed players. It's common for the top three customers to be half of revenue. That's fine while things are good, but one lost tender can move the whole year.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Is that a live risk at Stellan?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Their biggest customer has given notice on the five-year supply deal. That's about a fifth of revenue, and the market doesn't know.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Let's talk about sustainability. How is the plastic packaging tax changing demand?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: It's pushing customers towards recycled content and paper-based formats. Suppliers that secured recycled resin early are winning share, and the others are either paying the tax or losing the work.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: What about automation in packaging plants?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Mostly in quality inspection now. Camera systems catch print and seal defects that people used to miss, and that cuts customer complaints. It's a quick payback, often under two years.

missed-nadia-rahimi.reviewer_comment: The expert left Stellan, a listed company, only in August and disclosed that its largest customer has given notice on a contract worth about a fifth of revenue, which she says the market does not know. We redacted the passage and referred the expert to the vetting team.
missed-nadia-rahimi.root_cause: The AI's log scored the turn as a continuation of the expert's general point about customer concentration and labelled it an illustrative industry example. It gave no weight to 'the market doesn't know' and did not check that she had left Stellan, a listed company, three months before the call.
missed-nadia-rahimi.name: Nadia Rahimi
missed-nadia-rahimi.role: Account Manager, Fenwick Cartons (2014 to 2018). Key Account Director, Stellan Packaging (2018 to August 2026). Independent packaging consultant (August 2026 to present).

missed-benjamin-cole.profile: Benjamin Cole. Regional Sales Manager, Hartwell Pumps (2014 to 2021). Commercial Director, Ridgeway Industrial Supply (2021 to present). Industry: industrial equipment distribution.
missed-benjamin-cole.declaration: Currently employed by Ridgeway Industrial Supply, the main UK distributor for Corran Engineering (listed company). May discuss the industrial equipment market in general. Must not share Ridgeway's or Corran's non-public sales, order or pricing data.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Benjamin, thanks for joining. I'm looking at demand for industrial pumps and valves in the UK. How does the market feel?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Subdued. Water companies are spending, because the new regulatory period has a big investment programme, but general manufacturing has been cautious all year. Customers are repairing rather than replacing where they can.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: How much of the market goes through distributors?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Most of the smaller orders. Manufacturers sell large engineered pumps direct, but standard units and spares go through distributors, who hold stock and offer next-day delivery. It's really a service business.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: What are you seeing on pricing?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Manufacturers pushed through big increases in 2022 and 2023. This year it's been flat to slightly up. Customers are asking two or three suppliers for quotes before they order.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: How do you see Corran heading into the year end?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: I'd expect them to miss guidance. The October order book I saw was down about 15% on last year.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Turning to water, how long will that investment cycle run?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Five years at least, and the spending is weighted towards the later years. Water companies are under pressure on leaks and sewage overflows, so pumping stations and network upgrades are high on the list. Contractors are more of a bottleneck than equipment.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Any view on energy efficiency rules?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: They help replacement demand. Older motors and pumps can use far more energy than modern variable-speed units, so customers with high power bills can justify a swap on payback alone.

missed-benjamin-cole.reviewer_comment: As Corran's main distributor, the expert has access to its order data, and he disclosed a non-public order book trend that points to a guidance miss at a listed company. We redacted the passage and reminded the expert of his restrictions.
missed-benjamin-cole.root_cause: The AI logged 'I'd expect them to miss guidance' as the expert's own forecast and classified the passage as opinion. It folded the 15% figure into that view and missed that 'the order book I saw' means he had seen Corran's internal data through the distribution relationship set out in his declaration.
missed-benjamin-cole.name: Benjamin Cole
missed-benjamin-cole.role: Regional Sales Manager, Hartwell Pumps (2014 to 2021). Commercial Director, Ridgeway Industrial Supply (2021 to present).

missed-priya-natarajan.profile: Priya Natarajan. VP Sales EMEA, Teallight Software (2021 to present). Previously Sales Director, Orbisoft (2016 to 2021). Industry: B2B SaaS, workforce scheduling software.
missed-priya-natarajan.declaration: Currently employed by Teallight Software (private company). May discuss the workforce software market, buyer behaviour and competitors in general terms. Must not share Teallight's non-public pricing, roadmap or customer information.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Priya, thanks for joining. I'm looking at the workforce scheduling software market in Europe. How would you describe demand right now?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Healthy but more scrutinised. Two years ago, buyers were adding tools quickly. Now every purchase goes through finance, and they want a clear payback, usually within a year.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Who are the typical buyers?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Operations leaders in retail, hospitality and healthcare. HR is involved, but operations owns the budget because scheduling directly drives labour cost, which is often their biggest line.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: How competitive is pricing?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Competitive at the low end, where you have lots of simple tools. At the enterprise end, it's more about integration with payroll and time-and-attendance systems. Switching costs are high once you're integrated.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Are vendors pushing price increases?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Most of the market is trying. For us specifically, we're moving list price up 12% on the mid-market tier from January. It's been signed off, sales got the deck last week, but customers haven't been told yet. We think churn risk is low because of the integrations.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Interesting. How do buyers usually react to increases like that?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: In general, they push back, then accept if the vendor shows new value at the same time, a new module or better reporting. The ones who churn are usually the smaller accounts who were price shopping anyway.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: What about AI features in scheduling?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Everyone is adding demand forecasting. The useful version predicts footfall or patient volume and builds a draft rota. The hype version is a chatbot on top. Buyers are getting better at telling the difference.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Which segment is growing fastest?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Healthcare. Staffing pressures are severe, agency costs are high, and better scheduling reduces agency spend directly. That's an easy business case.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Thank you, Priya.

missed-priya-natarajan.reviewer_comment: Non-public pricing decision at the expert's current employer, not yet told to customers, in breach of her declaration. Redacted; the expert gets a reminder of her restrictions.
missed-priya-natarajan.root_cause: The AI only checks passages that name a company. This one says “for us”, and linking that to Teallight, her current employer, needs her declaration, which the AI didn't read.
missed-priya-natarajan.name: Priya Natarajan
missed-priya-natarajan.role: VP Sales EMEA, Teallight Software (2021 to present). Previously Sales Director, Orbisoft (2016 to 2021).

missed-grace-liu.profile: Grace Liu. Production Engineer, Thornbury Plastics (2015 to 2020). Operations Director, Kelsall Home Products (2020 to present). Industry: household goods manufacturing.
missed-grace-liu.declaration: Currently employed by Kelsall Home Products (private company). May discuss UK manufacturing trends in general. Must not share Kelsall's non-public plans, site decisions, financials or customer information.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Grace, thanks for your time. I'm researching UK manufacturers of household goods. What's the biggest pressure on them at the moment?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Energy and labour, in that order. Moulding and finishing use a lot of power, and contracts signed in 2022 and 2023 are only now rolling off. Wages have also risen fast, especially for skilled maintenance engineers.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: How are manufacturers responding?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Consolidating sites. A lot of these businesses grew by acquisition and ended up with four or five small plants. Running two bigger, more automated ones is cheaper, even after redundancy and moving costs.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Is that happening across the sector?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Broadly, yes. Most mid-sized groups have a footprint review going on. The north west has been hit hardest, because many of the older plants are there.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Are you seeing that in your own business?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: We're closing the Manchester plant in March. The staff haven't been told yet, so please keep that between us.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Understood. Back to the wider market, how do retailers behave as customers?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: They're tough. They want lower prices and smaller, more frequent deliveries. Manufacturers with good forecasting and flexible lines cope. The ones that run long batches end up holding stock.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Where does automation make the most sense?

turns.text: Is technology changing the junior roles?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Yes. Document review and first drafts are increasingly done with software, so trainees do client work earlier. Firms are rethinking how they train people when the routine tasks are gone.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: What would you tell a firm planning to expand in the north?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Hire a respected local partner first. Lawyers follow people, not brands, and a known name brings a team and clients with them.

false-alarm-chloe-martin.reviewer_comment: Fenmore announced the Leeds office in a public press release in September, which we confirmed on its website. The expert is repeating public news about her employer, so we cleared it.
false-alarm-chloe-martin.root_cause: The AI's employer rule fired on 'we' together with a new office, which it matched to the declaration's ban on Fenmore's non-public plans. It did not check the press release the expert cites, which Fenmore published the month before the call.

false-alarm-chloe-martin.role: Recruitment Consultant, Harrowgate Partners (2014 to 2020). Head of Talent, Fenmore Legal Services (2020 to present).

false-alarm-ibrahim-yusuf.profile: Ibrahim Yusuf. Implementation Consultant, Corbridge Systems (2015 to 2019). Head of Customer Success, Tidewell Software (2019 to present). Industry: B2B SaaS, field service management.
false-alarm-ibrahim-yusuf.declaration: Currently employed by Tidewell Software (private company). May discuss the field service software market in general. Must not share Tidewell's non-public pricing, roadmap or customer information.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Ibrahim, thanks for joining. I'm looking at software for field service teams: plumbers, electricians, maintenance firms. Who's buying?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Mostly firms with ten to two hundred engineers. Below that, people get by with spreadsheets and a shared calendar. Above that, they tend to buy enterprise systems with long implementations.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: What drives the purchase?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Scheduling and getting paid. If engineers can see their jobs on a phone, take photos and collect payment on site, the office spends less time chasing invoices. That's the business case most owners understand.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: How do vendors price these tools?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Mostly per user per month, with a basic, standard and premium tier. Add-ons like payments or route planning are where vendors try to grow revenue.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Where does Tidewell sit on price?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Our prices are on the website. The standard tier is £40 a seat, and that hasn't changed this year.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: How sticky are customers once they're on a system?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Fairly sticky. Once job history and customer records are in, moving is painful. Churn is mostly very small firms that close or shrink, not customers leaving for a competitor.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: What's the next big feature?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Smarter scheduling that accounts for traffic, engineer skills and the parts on the van. Most firms still plan the day by hand each morning.

false-alarm-ibrahim-yusuf.reviewer_comment: The £40 standard tier is on Tidewell's public pricing page, which we checked. A published list price is not confidential, so we cleared it.
false-alarm-ibrahim-yusuf.root_cause: The AI keyed on a precise price for the expert's current employer, 'our' plus '£40 a seat', and matched it to the declaration's ban on non-public pricing. It did not treat 'Our prices are on the website' as a source to check, and so did not tell a published list price apart from internal pricing.
false-alarm-ibrahim-yusuf.name: Ibrahim Yusuf

false-alarm-ruth-okonkwo.profile: Ruth Okonkwo. Environmental Engineer, Ashby Aggregates (2014 to 2021). Head of Sustainability, Marchbank Building Materials (2021 to present). Industry: construction materials.
false-alarm-ruth-okonkwo.declaration: Currently employed by Marchbank Building Materials (private company). May discuss decarbonisation in the building materials sector in general. Must not share Marchbank's non-public data, plans or customer information.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Ruth, thanks for your time. I'm looking at how building materials producers are cutting emissions. Where does the industry stand?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Early, but moving. Cement and lime are the hard part, because most of the emissions come from the chemistry, not just the fuel. Bricks, blocks and aggregates are easier: it's mostly a question of energy and transport.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Can you share anything on your own company's progress?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: I can only tell you what's in our published sustainability report: we cut emissions by about a tenth last year. Most of that came from switching kilns to lower-carbon fuels, which the report also describes.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: What are the main levers for the sector?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Alternative fuels in kilns, cement blends with less clinker, and electric plant and vehicles at quarries. Carbon capture is the big one for cement, but it needs pipelines and storage that don't exist at scale yet.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Are customers paying more for lower-carbon products?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Some are. Large contractors and public clients increasingly ask for carbon data in tenders. Housebuilders are more driven by price, though that's changing as building rules tighten.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: How is carbon pricing affecting the sector?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: It makes the business case for capture and fuel switching much clearer. A carbon levy on imports also matters, because it should stop cheaper, higher-carbon imports undercutting domestic producers.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Thanks, Ruth.

false-alarm-ruth-okonkwo.reviewer_comment: The figure comes straight from Marchbank's published sustainability report, which the expert names, and the report confirms an emissions cut of about a tenth. Public information, so we cleared it.
false-alarm-ruth-okonkwo.root_cause: The AI's log shows it split the sentence at the colon and assessed 'we cut emissions by about a tenth last year' on its own, as a quantified internal metric about the current employer. The attribution to the published sustainability report sat in the first half of the sentence and was lost.
false-alarm-ruth-okonkwo.name: Ruth Okonkwo
false-alarm-ruth-okonkwo.role: Environmental Engineer, Ashby Aggregates (2014 to 2021). Head of Sustainability, Marchbank Building Materials (2021 to present).

false-alarm-marco-rossi.profile: Marco Rossi. Product Designer, Albaro Elettrodomestici (2013 to 2019). Senior Product Manager, Velmora Home Appliances (2019 to present). Industry: domestic appliances.
false-alarm-marco-rossi.declaration: Currently employed by Velmora Home Appliances (private company). May discuss the domestic appliance market in general. Must not share Velmora's non-public product plans, pricing or sales data.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Marco, thanks for joining. I'm researching connected kitchen appliances in Europe. Is there real demand?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: For some products, yes. Ovens with cameras and guided cooking sell well at the premium end. Connected fridges, much less so. Most buyers don't see the point of a screen on the fridge door.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: What do consumers actually value?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Saving time and energy. Preheating remotely, alerts when a cycle finishes, and seeing energy use. Recipes and apps matter less than the industry hoped.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Is Velmora doing anything in this area?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Our chief executive showed the new product on stage at the trade show in September, so it's public now. It's the connected oven from the press coverage, and I'll stick to what was shown there.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: How are retailers selling these products?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Mostly through kitchen showrooms and big electrical retailers. Demonstrations matter, because people need to see the camera and app working before they pay a premium.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: What about price pressure from Asian brands?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: It's strong in the mid-market. European brands are holding on through design, service networks and longer warranties, but the gap on features has closed.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Where do you see the market in five years?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Connectivity will be standard and nobody will pay extra for it. The value will move to energy management, especially as more homes get solar panels and time-of-use tariffs.

false-alarm-marco-rossi.reviewer_comment: The oven was launched on stage at a public trade show in September and covered in the trade press, and the expert stuck to what was shown there. Nothing confidential, so we cleared it.
false-alarm-marco-rossi.root_cause: The AI matched 'new product' to the declaration's ban on non-public product plans and read 'so it's public now' as the expert justifying a disclosure, a pattern its rules mark as higher risk. It did not check the September trade show, where the oven was shown on stage and widely reported.
false-alarm-marco-rossi.name: Marco Rossi
false-alarm-marco-rossi.role: Product Designer, Albaro Elettrodomestici (2013 to 2019). Senior Product Manager, Velmora Home Appliances (2019 to present).
